newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH MONEY RATES UNDER UPWARD PRESSURE.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH MONEY RATES UNDER UPWARD PRESSURE.

text.p: Dutch call money rates remained under upward pressure on Wednesday because market players are still not completely familiar with new instruments introduced last Friday by the central bank.

Banks must now maintain a compulsory cash reserve with the central bank, the average size of which is set in advance for a period of four to five weeks. The central bank said this system should stabilise money market rates.
"Players still have to get used to the new instruments and to me it seems that call money rates are going to fluctuate even more," said one dealer.
Call money was bid between 3.12 and 3.18 percent today versus 3.12 on Tuesday.
Under the previous system, call money was usually bid just above the special advances rate, currently 2.90 percent.
Under that system, call money could fluctuate widely towards the expiry of the three monthly credit quota if commercial banks used up too much liquidity under the quota or had been saving too much.
"Call money is likely to fluctuate more as the cash reserve is set for a period for four to five weeks," said one dealer.
He said this probably meant that call money would fall strongly once a month, towards the end of each cash reserve arrangement.
"I foresee the same kind of lows (for call rates) as we used to see once every three months under the old credit quota," the dealer said.
Just ahead of the last three-monthly credit quota in the preceding week, call money rates dipped to a low of 1.50 percent bid.
The dealer said banks were more careful in planning their call money business as they are no longer allowed to show a debit balance at the end of the day.
"That makes it more difficult for banks to bet on the amount of liquidity they need for the day," said one dealer.

Another dealer said market players needed more time to get used to the new money market instruments, which were introduced last week to bring Dutch money market policy more in line with Europe as part of monetary union.
Three month deposits were two basis points higher at 3.16 percent bid.
The guilder was slightly weaker versus the German mark, trading at 112.49 per 100 marks from 112.445 on Tuesday.
